client: I've been feeling really anxious ever since my professor assigned this big group presentation project. The thought of having to speak in front of the whole class makes my stomach turn, and I'm already worrying about letting my group down because of my nerves. I'm not sure talking about it will help since the presentation is unavoidable, but I can't stop thinking about it.
therapist: It sounds like this presentation is bringing up a lot of worry for you, especially about how your anxiety might affect your group. When these anxious thoughts come up, what specific concerns run through your mind about the situation?

client: I keep imagining myself freezing up during the presentation and letting my group down. The worst part is thinking about their disappointed faces if I mess up - like they'll see me as incompetent or unreliable. I know it's irrational, but I can't shake this fear that one bad performance will ruin all my work relationships.
therapist: I hear how deeply this fear of judgment is affecting you - that worry about disappointing others can feel so heavy. Let's examine this thought together: what evidence do you have that one presentation would actually ruin all your relationships?

client: I get what you're saying about looking for evidence, but it's hard to shake this feeling. When I messed up a work presentation last month, I saw my boss's disappointed face and my coworkers stopped inviting me to lunch for weeks. It feels like one mistake can change how people see me permanently.
therapist: That sounds like a really painful experience that's understandably making this current situation feel even more daunting. Would it help to explore together how we might separate that past experience from this upcoming presentation - what differences do you notice between these two situations?

client: I guess the main difference is that this time I actually know the material well, unlike that disaster presentation in college where I was totally unprepared. But I still feel this heavy dread like my mind will go blank again, even though logically I know I'm more capable now. It's frustrating because part of me knows I'll probably be fine, but the anxiety feels just as intense as back then.
therapist: It's interesting how your anxiety feels just as strong now, even though you're actually much more prepared this time - that shows how powerful our emotional memories can be. What do you make of that gap between knowing you're capable and still feeling that same intense dread?

client:
It's frustrating because logically I know I can handle this work presentation, but my body still reacts like it's life or death. I keep remembering how I froze up last year, and even though I've practiced so much more now, that old panic just takes over. 

Part of me thinks I should just trust my preparation, but another part is convinced I'll mess up again no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real battle going on between your rational preparation and those powerful emotional memories from past experiences. When the panic starts to take over, what helps you notice that this is your anxiety speaking rather than a true reflection of your current abilities?

client:
Honestly, even when I know it's anxiety talking, it still feels so real in the moment. My chest gets tight and I start remembering all the times I failed before, and it's like my brain just ignores any evidence that I might do okay this time. 

Sometimes I try to tell myself "this is just anxiety," but it doesn't always help because the physical feelings are so strong. It's like my body is screaming danger no matter what my rational mind says.
therapist:
I hear how overwhelming it feels when your body's alarm system takes over, even when your rational mind knows the facts. That disconnect between what you know and what you feel can be so frustrating. 

When those physical symptoms start, have you noticed any small ways to create even a brief pause between the physical reaction and the spiral of anxious thoughts?

client:
I've tried taking deep breaths when I feel anxious, but sometimes it makes me more aware of how fast my heart is racing and then I panic even more. I know techniques like grounding are supposed to help, but in the moment it feels impossible to remember or do them right. 

Part of me worries that if I can't even do simple breathing exercises correctly, how am I supposed to handle bigger anxiety triggers?
therapist: It sounds like even the coping strategies meant to help can sometimes intensify your anxiety, which must feel really discouraging. That worry about "doing it right" seems particularly strong - what would it feel like to approach these techniques with curiosity rather than pressure to perform them perfectly?

client: I get what you're saying about curiosity, but it's hard to shift gears when my mind automatically goes to "I'm failing at this too." Like when I try deep breathing, I start overanalyzing whether I'm inhaling for the right count, and then I just feel more tense. The pressure comes from worrying that if I don't do it perfectly, my anxiety will never get better.
therapist:
I hear how this perfectionism is making it even harder to find relief from your anxiety - that automatic "I'm failing" thought adds another layer of stress when you're already feeling overwhelmed. 

What if we reframed the breathing exercises not as something you need to do perfectly, but as simple experiments to notice what happens in your body without judgment?

client:
I get what you're saying about not needing to do it perfectly, but that's easier said than done. Even just hearing "experiment" makes me anxious because I feel like I should be getting measurable results from it. 

I tried the breathing exercises yesterday and kept getting frustrated because my mind wouldn't stop racing. It made me feel like I was failing at something that's supposed to be simple.
therapist: It sounds like this frustration with the exercises is adding another layer of pressure, when what you really need is some relief. That "should" about measurable results seems particularly strong - what would it look like to approach these moments with just a tiny bit more self-compassion when things don't go as hoped?

client: I know self-compassion sounds nice in theory, but when I fail at these exercises, it just makes me feel like I'm failing at therapy too. That "should" about results is there because I've been struggling with anxiety for so long - if this doesn't work, what am I supposed to do? The thought of going easy on myself almost feels like giving up.
therapist:
I hear how deeply frustrating this struggle feels, and how the idea of self-compassion almost seems to clash with your determination to overcome this. That fear of "giving up" if you're not pushing yourself hard enough is completely understandable given how long you've been battling with this anxiety. 

Would it help to explore together what a middle ground might look like - between pushing too hard and giving up entirely? Perhaps there's a way to be both determined and gentle with yourself in this process?
